lesson.title: Beta-One: The Truth the Sample Line Is Chasing
lesson.summary: Beta1 is the fixed, unknown true slope of the population or process regression line, and everything in slope inference exists only to estimate and test claims about this one number.
lesson.body:
Every calculation and every condition in the last two chapters exists to answer one question: what is beta1, the true slope of the population or process regression line? Beta1 is a parameter in the same sense you have met parameters before, a fixed, numerical fact about an entire population or underlying process, unknown to us, that does not change from sample to sample. That is precisely what separates it from b1, the sample slope: b1 is a statistic, computed from whichever particular sample happened to get collected, and it would come out at least slightly different if a new sample were drawn. Every ounce of effort in slope inference, the standard error, the t-statistic, the confidence interval, exists only to say something honest about the one number we cannot directly observe, beta1, using the one number we can compute, b1.

In context, beta1 is the true average change in the response variable for every one-unit increase in the explanatory variable, across the entire population or process, not just the six students who happened to be sampled. In the study hours example, beta1 would be the true average change in quiz score per additional hour studied, if you could somehow observe every student in the relevant population rather than just six of them. Since that is not possible, b1 equals 1.143 is our best single estimate of beta1, and the earlier 95% confidence interval, roughly 0.39 to 1.90, is our estimate of a plausible range for the actual value of beta1. That interval is wide because n equals 6 is tiny. A larger sample would typically shrink the standard error and narrow the interval, giving a more precise fix on beta1 without changing what beta1 itself means.

The value beta1 equals 0 carries special meaning: it describes a population in which the true regression line is perfectly flat, meaning y does not actually depend on x at all, and any apparent pattern in a sample would just be noise. That is exactly why H0: beta1 equals 0 is the standard null hypothesis for slope inference, no linear relationship in the population, and why rejecting it, as the study hours example did with a P-value of about 0.014, counts as evidence that beta1 truly is not zero: some real linear relationship exists in the population or process being studied, not just an accident of this particular sample.

Beta1's sign and size both carry information that a correlation coefficient alone does not. Correlation r is unitless and only describes strength and direction. Beta1 has units, here, quiz score points per hour studied, and describes an actual rate of change. A positive beta1, as estimated here, means quiz scores genuinely tend to rise with more hours studied in this population. The size of beta1, about 1.14 points per hour based on this sample, estimates how large that true average increase really is.
